clue.text: Flora, say, hindered 26 by wire

indicators.note: the answer to 26 across means turned upside down, which in a down entry flips the preceding words from bottom to top

blocks.note: Flora is a brand of margarine, and marge is the British short form of margarine
to let is an old verb meaning to hinder, as in 'without let or hindrance'

explanation.surface: A woman called Flora is held up by a fence of wire.
explanation.walkthrough: MARGE + LET is read upwards to give TELEGRAM. Flora is a margarine sold in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: A telegram was a message sent by telegraph, so a wire is an informal name for one.

clue.text: Shakespeare, perhaps, or Bacon?

blocks.note: first meaning: a poet, Shakespeare being the ... of Avon
second meaning: a thin rasher of bacon or fat tied over meat before roasting

explanation.walkthrough: The surface alludes to the theory that Francis Bacon wrote Shakespeare's plays; the question mark flags that the second sense is the cookery one.
explanation.definitionFit: A poet is called a bard, and in cooking a bard is a slice of fat laid over lean meat.

clue.text: Jewish spice gives lift to alien musical

indicators.note: in a down entry, lifting the words raises them so they read from the bottom upwards

blocks.note: ET is the film's extraterrestrial, the crossword's usual alien
Cats is the Lloyd Webber musical

explanation.surface: A spice from Jewish tradition boosts the fortunes of a show about an alien.
explanation.walkthrough: ET + CATS read upwards gives STACTE.
explanation.definitionFit: Stacte was one of the sweet spices of the holy incense described in Exodus, so it is fairly a Jewish spice.

clue.text: Malicious gossip fell on cultivated land

indicators.note: ground that is cultivated has been turned over and broken up, so these letters are dug into a new order

blocks.note: the setter's intended sense is unclear; these letters are left over once the cultivated land is accounted for
taken as written

explanation.surface: Nasty rumour descended upon a farmer's fields.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram of LAND gives the ending NDAL; how 'fell' supplies SCA is not clear, and the clue is best taken as a loose hint at SCANDAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Scandal is talk that damages someone's reputation, the very thing malicious gossip spreads.

clue.text: A teach-in, first to last on drink

indicators.note: the opening portion of the phrase is moved to the back, so it now comes last instead of first

blocks.note: taken as written, split as A TEA and CHIN

explanation.surface: A seminar session is run on refreshments.
explanation.walkthrough: Read A TEACH-IN as A TEA + CHIN, then send the first part to the end.
explanation.definitionFit: China tea is tea grown in China, a familiar hot beverage served without milk.

clue.text: Kinky model in parsonage providing a show up front

indicators.note: something kinky is twisted, so the letters of the vicar's house are twisted into a new order
one piece is placed inside the other, sitting within its letters

blocks.note: the Model T was Ford's famous car
taken as written

explanation.surface: A scandalous model at the vicar's house puts on a racy display.
explanation.walkthrough: T goes into a rearrangement of PARSONAGE to make APRON STAGE.
explanation.definitionFit: An apron stage projects in front of the proscenium arch, so the performance happens out in front of the curtain.

clue.text: Norman armour used by the sovereign

blocks.note: mail is armour of linked rings, as in chain mail
ER is Elizabeth Regina, the Queen

explanation.surface: Chain mail of the Norman conquerors worn by the king.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Norman' looks like an adjective for the armour of 1066, but it is a first name.
explanation.definitionFit: Norman Mailer was the American novelist, so his first name stands for his surname here.

clue.text: It means many are confused about meaning

indicators.note: words that are confused are muddled up, so their letters come out in a jumbled order
the jumbled letters go around the other piece, enclosing it

blocks.note: taken as written
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, a large number

explanation.surface: A grammarian notes that a phrase means several people are puzzled about what words signify.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram letters wrap around C here only at the end, so 'about' is loose; 'about meaning' doubles as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Semantic describes anything concerned with the sense of words, so it means relating to meaning.

clue.text: Magnificent group knowing a little?

blocks.note: hep is an old slang word for being in the know, like hip
a tad is a small amount

explanation.surface: A splendid band who know just a bit.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition alludes to the film The Magnificent Seven.
explanation.definitionFit: A heptad is a set of seven, so the Magnificent Seven form one.

clue.text: Tuesday or Wednesday, when pupil comes in

indicators.note: the learner arrives inside the day, entering between its letters

blocks.note: Wed is the standard abbreviation for Wednesday
L for learner, as on British learner-driver plates

explanation.surface: Asking which weekday a new pupil starts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tuesday' looks like a day of the week but is the first name of the actress Tuesday Weld.
explanation.definitionFit: Tuesday Weld is an American film actress, so her first name points to her surname.

clue.text: Once no lady could become a writer

indicators.note: the letters are said to turn into something else, so they are rearranged to form a new name

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: In the old days a woman could not take up authorship.
explanation.definitionFit: Arthur Conan Doyle was the author who created Sherlock Holmes, so he is a well-known man of letters.

clue.text: Flinch from having bell in church

indicators.note: the bell sits inside the church, so one piece lies within the other

blocks.note: CE is the Church of England
a ring is a telephone call, as in 'give me a bell'

explanation.surface: Someone recoils at the noise of the church bell.
explanation.definitionFit: To cringe is to shrink back in fear or embarrassment, the same reflex as a flinch.

clue.text: City man upset over tonight's performance

indicators.note: something upset is knocked over and disordered, so these letters are thrown about
a performance is a production, so the letters are put on in a different form

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man is distressed about this evening's show in town.
explanation.walkthrough: Both MAN and TONIGHT are rearranged together.
explanation.definitionFit: Nottingham is a city in the English East Midlands, home of the Robin Hood legend.

clue.text: Attempt sitar badly before achieving creative elegance

indicators.note: an instrument played badly comes out wrong, so its letters come out in the wrong order

blocks.note: taken as written
a try is an attempt

explanation.surface: A musician plays the sitar poorly before eventually mastering it.
explanation.walkthrough: The scrambled sitar comes before TRY even though the attempt is named first.
explanation.definitionFit: Artistry is creative skill and grace in execution, so it matches creative elegance.

clue.text: Wounded boy turns in his gun

indicators.note: the boy turns round, so his name faces the other way
the turned name goes inside the weapon

blocks.note: a boy's name, short for Timothy
the Sten is a British submachine gun

explanation.surface: An injured lad turns his weapon on himself.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sten was a British submachine gun of the Second World War.
explanation.definitionFit: Smitten is the past participle of smite, so it means struck down or injured.

clue.text: Master European currency (gold)

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for European
the ducat was a gold coin used across Europe
or is gold in heraldry

explanation.surface: A financial master explains the single European currency backed by gold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'European currency' wants to be the euro, but it splits into E and DUCAT.
explanation.definitionFit: A master in the old sense is a schoolteacher, and an educator is one who teaches.

clue.text: New Year honours for a composer

blocks.note: January begins the new year
ace and king (K) are honours, the top cards in bridge

explanation.surface: Someone gets a knighthood in the New Year honours list for musical services.
explanation.walkthrough: The New Year Honours list is Britain's annual roll of awards, but here honours are the top cards of a bridge hand.
explanation.definitionFit: Leos Janacek was the Czech composer of Jenufa and the Sinfonietta.

clue.text: The elder displayed another millennium disaster

indicators.note: something displayed is laid out for show, here in a fresh arrangement of the letters

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An old man showed off yet another calamity at the turn of the millennium.
explanation.walkthrough: Written as the Millennium Bug and Dome fears ran high: Ethelred the Unready, the English king around AD 1000, was unready for the last one.
explanation.definitionFit: Ethelred the Unready reigned at the first millennium and his rule was a byword for failure.

clue.text: Cards involving complicated quiz in spelling test

indicators.note: a complicated thing is tangled, so the letters are tangled up
the test involves the jumbled word, taking it inside

blocks.note: taken as written
a spelling bee is a spelling contest

explanation.surface: A card round turns up as a tricky question in a spelling test.
explanation.definitionFit: Bezique is a card game for two players using a double pack of cards.

clue.text: It is lowered for landing

blocks.note: surface reading: something lowered before touching down, like an aircraft's wheels
setter's reading: the plane's height above the ground is reduced to land

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests undercarriage or flaps; the thing lowered is the plane's height itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Altitude is height above sea level or ground, which a pilot must reduce to bring the aircraft down.

clue.text: They grow to be worthy of consideration

definitions.text: They grow to be worthy of consideration

blocks.clueFragment: They grow to be worthy of consideration
blocks.note: surface reading: people who mature into someone worth taking seriously
setter's reading: the flowers of the Sermon on the Mount, 'Consider ... of the field, how they grow'

explanation.walkthrough: Matthew 6:28 says 'Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow', so these are the plants one is told to consider.
explanation.definitionFit: Lilies are flowers, and the Gospel verse makes them the things that grow and are worth considering.

clue.text: The ego trip for a poet?

indicators.note: a trip is a stumble or a drug-fuelled disorientation, so the letters are thrown off balance into new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Is a poet merely on an ego trip?
explanation.definitionFit: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe was the German poet and dramatist who wrote Faust.

clue.text: State measure for reproductive material

blocks.note: GA is the abbreviation for Georgia, a US state
to mete is to measure out

explanation.surface: A government sets a rule on reproductive biology.
explanation.definitionFit: A gamete is a sex cell, egg or sperm, the material that fuses in reproduction.

clue.text: "Pam is a girl" - unfortunately that's been used before

indicators.note: an unfortunate phrase has gone wrong, so its letters are misarranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Pointing out that a hackneyed line has been written before.
explanation.definitionFit: Plagiarism is passing off another's work as one's own, writing that has already been used by someone else.

clue.text: Daring to speak of a way out

indicators.note: speaking the next words out means their sound is what counts

blocks.note: being bowled is one of the ways a batsman is out in cricket

explanation.surface: Being brave enough to mention an escape route.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A way out' sounds like an exit, but in cricket a batsman is out when bowled, the ball hitting the stumps.
explanation.definitionFit: Bold means brave and fearless, the same quality as daring.

clue.text: Sound prospect for conveyance of neat dwelling

indicators.note: the sound of the following words matters, not how they are written

blocks.note: in a property sale, conveyance transfers the house to the prospective purchaser

explanation.surface: A sound prospect for a property deal on a tidy house.
explanation.walkthrough: Neat is an old word for cattle, so a neat dwelling is not a tidy home but a cowshed.
explanation.definitionFit: A byre is a cowshed, the place where cattle, or neat, are housed.

clue.text: Smooth diplomat stops short at nothing

indicators.note: the envoy halts before the end, so the final letter is missing

blocks.note: a legate is an ambassador or papal envoy
O looks like zero

explanation.surface: A suave diplomat will stop at nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface twists 'stops at nothing', meaning ruthless.
explanation.definitionFit: Legato is the musical direction to play notes smoothly joined, with no breaks between them.

clue.text: Showing improvement when put under treatment

indicators.note: something given treatment is worked on and altered, so the letters are reworked

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A patient gets better after being anaesthetised for surgery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put under' suggests anaesthesia, but it is the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that has upturned has taken an upward turn, so it is getting better.
